claims.text: An actively trained machine-learning interatomic potential integrated with free-energy perturbation can yield fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties.
The proposed method can achieve accuracy close to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed method can substantially reduce computational cost relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
Active learning can refine the ML potential sufficiently to capture anharmonic vibrational contributions.
Active learning can refine the ML potential sufficiently to capture electron-vibration coupling effects.
Vibrational anharmonicity and electronic effects are significant near the phase transition.
Relevant near-transition calculations are typically performed a few hundred kelvin below the melting point.
The ML training remains reliable under the stated near-transition conditions.
The potential's descriptors and training protocol can accurately represent local atomic environments across solid and fluid phases.
The learned representation accurately describes the vibrational and electronic interactions connecting the solid and fluid phases.
Replacing extensive ab initio molecular dynamics with ML evaluations reduces computational cost.
Free-energy perturbation retains the essential entropy and anharmonicity effects needed for thermodynamic fidelity.
The method will reproduce phase free energies and fusion-temperature estimates within approximately 5–10% relative error of explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The method will provide a computational speed-up of approximately 10–100 times relative to TOR-TILD.
The method is applicable to elemental, binary, and moderately complex multicomponent alloys near fusion conditions.
Reliability may degrade in extreme high-entropy systems or under strongly anharmonic conditions.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis repeatedly places calculations near the fusion point, but the conditions characterize this as typically a few hundred kelvin below the melting point. Under equilibrium usage, fusion and melting temperatures denote the same transition, so this temperature boundary is internally ambiguous.
